items.title: Segments: Atlas of a Data Leak
items.note: Albrecht took a leaked set of over 650,000 audience segments from 93 data brokers and mapped them. These are the boxes people get sorted into by behaviour, mood and even morals. 330 pages, 97 diagrams, set in Monument Grotesk. The closest thing to your day job on this list, and a sobering one.

items.title: Karel Martens: Cloakroom Tickets
items.note: Martens kept a booklet of numbered cloakroom tickets in his studio for years, meaning to print over it one day. He finally did: 50 monoprints, reproduced front and back at actual size. A quieter, odder companion to his 2027 calendar.

items.title: Saâdane Afif: Affiches 2
items.note: The first book given over entirely to Afif's posters, in an expanded edition from Triangle Books in Brussels. Each poster was made for a show or performance and carries its title, date and collaborators, so together they read as an archive of his work. 176 pages, 24 x 32 cm. A good case for the poster as a record, not just an announcement.

items.title: Assume Nothing: On Practice-Based Art, Design and Education
items.note: Projects by 32 recent graduates of the design and art faculty in Bolzano, paired with new essays on teaching. The idea is that not knowing is a working condition, not a failing. Designed by Melani De Luca, 224 pages. Worth a look if you mentor people early in their careers.

items.title: Fine Design: A Studio Guide to Remixing Design, Art, Craft, and Industry
items.note: Twenty years of studio teaching boiled down into essays and workbook-style exercises, about design that sits between art, craft and industry. Foreword by Andrew Blauvelt. It leans towards objects rather than graphics, but the exercises would work with any team.

items.title: Street Report 7: Naptime
items.note: Singapore is often called one of the most sleep-deprived countries in the world. Zohri watched people napping in public, on commutes, at lunch and between shifts, and turned it into explanatory drawings and short texts. A small 144-page paperback. Gentle, funny, and a nice bit of observational information design.

items.title: The National Grid #9
items.by: Luke Wood, Katie Kerr and Matthew Galloway
items.note: A graphic design journal from Aotearoa New Zealand, "occasionally looking elsewhere". Edited and designed by Luke Wood, Katie Kerr and Matthew Galloway, 112 pages, co-published with GLORIA Books. A way into a design scene that rarely reaches London.

items.title: Tools #6: To Blow
items.note: A Paris annual about making, this time on air and breath. Objects made from balloons, a history of inflatable buildings, crystal glassblowing at Saint-Louis, and an essay on breathlessness and bad air. Art directed by Twice studio, 248 pages, French and English. Calm, well paced pages.

items.title: Tinted #1
items.note: A new non-profit annual from Copenhagen that keeps AI-generated content out. Issue one, The Illusion of Hierarchy, is about the gap between what people do and who they are: six interviews, a cover story on veins, an essay on armour. Edited and art directed by Ida Yndal, openbound, 216 pages.

items.title: Daan Rietbergen
items.note: Utrecht designer who worked at Studio Dumbar and came away with a love of grids and systems. His heavy letterforms turn up on posters and as painted murals, including his Nespor typeface on walls in Amsterdam, Utrecht and Eindhoven. A clear line back to Crouwel, with more swagger. Follow for the posters and the walls.
